tip_title: Life Insurance Isn't Just About Replacing Your Income. There's Another Number Most People Forget.
topic: Life Insurance - Final Expense and Estate Settlement Costs
blurb:
💡 **Insurance Tip: Life Insurance Isn't Just About Replacing Your Income. There's Another Number Most People Forget.**

Most people think about life insurance as an income replacement tool — enough to cover years of lost earnings for a spouse or kids. That part makes sense. But there's a second bucket of costs that often gets left out of the calculation entirely: the expenses that come with settling an estate. Funeral costs, probate fees, taxes on transferred assets, and legal administrative costs can add up to a meaningful sum on top of whatever debt and income-replacement needs your family already has. The Insurance Information Institute recommends planning for at least $15,000 in final expense costs alone, and that's a floor, not a ceiling. If you haven't revisited your coverage amount recently, it's worth checking whether your current policy accounts for both sides of that equation.

Not sure if your life insurance number still makes sense for your situation? Your Peachy agent can help you think through it — no pressure, just a conversation.

📖 [Learn more from the Insurance Information Institute](https://www.iii.org/article/how-much-life-insurance-do-i-need)
summary: Covers the estate settlement cost component of life insurance adequacy — specifically funeral, probate, and administrative costs that are typically excluded from standard income-replacement calculations — framed as a coverage-completeness check distinct from prior income-replacement and college-funding angles.
scoring_notes: Prior life insurance tips have covered income replacement (Jun 22), beneficiary review (Jun 14, Apr 22), college funding (Aug 31), term vs. whole (Jul 27), and open enrollment/marriage (Sep 7). This is a genuinely different angle — estate settlement costs as a forgotten second line item in the coverage calculation. Fits both audiences well: East Cobb skews older with more established estates to consider; Perimeter and Lewisville Lake have younger professionals starting to accumulate assets. Evergreen but substantively distinct from prior tips. Trusted source: iii.org. Specific dollar reference ($15,000) is pulled directly from the source, not an invented figure.

tip_title: Your Home Policy Probably Doesn't Cover a Backed-Up Sewer. Most People Find That Out Too Late.
topic: Home Insurance - Sewer Backup Coverage Gap
blurb:
💡 **Insurance Tip: Your Home Policy Probably Doesn't Cover a Backed-Up Sewer. Most People Find That Out Too Late.**

Standard homeowners policies exclude sewer backup damage — meaning if a heavy rain overwhelms your municipal system and sewage comes up through your drains, you're looking at a cleanup bill your policy won't touch. It's one of the more common claims homeowners try to file after a big storm, and one of the more common denials. The fix is a sewer backup endorsement, which is typically inexpensive and can be added to most existing policies with a quick call. October storms are still very much on the table in Georgia and North Texas — so if you've never checked whether this is on your policy, now is a good time to look.

Not sure if sewer backup coverage is part of your policy? Your Peachy agent can check your declarations page and add it if it's missing.

📖 [Learn more from the Insurance Information Institute](https://www.iii.org/article/hurricane-season-insurance-guide)
summary: Covers the sewer backup exclusion in standard homeowners policies — that sewage damage from overwhelmed municipal systems is not covered — and the endorsement that closes that gap, framed as a post-storm-season awareness tip.
scoring_notes: High homeowner populations in both East Cobb (78%) and Lewisville Lake (65%) make this broadly relevant. Sewer backup has never been the primary subject of a prior tip — prior home endorsement tips (Aug 17, Sep 29) covered sewer backup only as one item in a list of endorsements, never as the focused angle. This tip zeroes in on sewer backup specifically, with a storm-season trigger that fits October in both Georgia and North Texas. Actionable: one phone call to an agent. Trusted source: iii.org. No carrier names, no dollar figures.

tip_title: You Have Two Kinds of Deductibles on Your Policies. Most People Think They Have One.
topic: Insurance Deductibles - Flat vs. Percentage Across Policy Types
blurb:
💡 **Insurance Tip: You Have Two Kinds of Deductibles on Your Policies. Most People Think They Have One.**

Here's something most people never think about: your auto policy and your homeowners policy don't use the same kind of deductible. On your auto policy, your deductible is almost always a flat dollar amount — say $500 or $1,000. You know exactly what you owe before your insurer pays. On your homeowners policy, though, there are often two layers: a flat deductible for most claims, and a separate percentage-based deductible that kicks in specifically for wind, hail, or named-storm damage. That second number isn't $500. It's typically 1% to 5% of your dwelling coverage amount — which on a $400,000 home is anywhere from $4,000 to $20,000 out of pocket before a dollar of coverage applies. Both numbers are on your declarations page. Most people have looked at neither.

Not sure what your deductibles actually are across your home and auto policies? Your Peachy agent can pull both declarations pages and walk you through the numbers in one conversation.

📖 [Learn more from the Insurance Information Institute](https://www.iii.org/article/understanding-your-insurance-deductibles)
summary: Covers the functional difference between flat dollar deductibles (standard in auto policies) and percentage-based deductibles (common in homeowners policies for wind/hail), framed as a cross-policy comparison most policyholders have never made — distinct from prior tips focused on auto deductible review alone or storm-season deductible checks.
scoring_notes: Works for both East Cobb audiences — 78% homeownership rate means the percentage-deductible side lands hard, and virtually every household has an auto policy too. October is late hurricane season in Georgia so wind/hail deductible awareness still has seasonal teeth without being a repeat of the storm-prep framing. Fresh angle: cross-policy deductible type comparison (flat vs. percentage) rather than a single-policy deductible review or storm-season check. Prior auto deductible tip (July 18) was a general review prompt; prior hail/wind tips (June 12, Aug 24) were percentage-mechanic explainers in a storm context — this tip reframes both as a side-by-side across policy types, which no prior tip has done. iii.org is a trusted source per guardrails.
